subsection: 10. Case study: the impact of RTÉ, 1962–1972

notes.h: Background: radio, rival signals and the Ireland of the 1950s
notes.b: Irish television began late, after a long debate about whether and how the state should run it. It arrived in a country with an established state radio service, a Church that shaped public morals and a government keen to modernise.
points: Radio had been run by the state since 2RN opened in Dublin in 1926; it later became Radio Éireann and in the 1950s it was part of the Department of Posts and Telegraphs, so the minister in charge of post and telegraphs also oversaw broadcasting.

Before 1961 some viewers in the east, the north and along the coast could pick up BBC and Ulster Television signals from Britain and Northern Ireland (Ulster Television began in 1959), and this showed that Irish demand for television was growing.

Seán Lemass was Taoiseach (prime minister) from 1959 to 1966, and his government stressed economic modernisation and opening Ireland to outside influences, which made a national television service attractive; Jack Lynch succeeded him in November 1966.

The Catholic Church, led in Dublin by Archbishop John Charles McQuaid (Archbishop from 1940 to 1972), had great influence on morals, and the state censored books and films, meaning officially banned material it judged harmful. Television would test these limits.
notes.tip: Be ready to say that radio was already state-run and that foreign signals showed there was a demand for television.

notes.h: Establishing Telefís Éireann: the 1960 Act, funding and launch
notes.b: The government decided that television should be a national service under public control. The law that set it up also decided who would run it and what the broadcaster owed the state.
points: The Broadcasting Authority Act 1960 set up an Authority to run radio and the new television service; the government appointed its members, which gave ministers a strong influence over who ran broadcasting. The Authority became known as Radio Telefís Éireann (RTÉ).
The service was financed by licence fees (paid by households that owned a set) and by advertising, so RTÉ needed both public approval and commercial income.
The Authority was a statutory body, meaning one created and governed by law, not a government department, and the Act required it to be impartial in news and current affairs.
Telefís Éireann began broadcasting on 31 December 1961, and President Éamon de Valera spoke at the opening and warned that television had a great power for good and for ill.
Transmitters were built so that television reached most of the country within a few years, and by the early 1970s most households had a set, which is why its influence grew so fast.

Take care with names: Telefís Éireann was the television service launched in 1961, while RTÉ was the name of the Authority running both radio and television, and Radio Éireann was the older radio service.
notes.tip: Remember the dated facts that earn marks for a launch question: the 1960 Act, licence fees and advertising, and 31 December 1961 with de Valera's warning about television's power.

notes.h: Control, policy and the Lemass view
notes.b: RTÉ was meant to be independent, yet the state kept strong powers over it. This tension between public service and government influence runs through the whole case study.
points: Section 31 of the Act let the Minister for Posts and Telegraphs direct the Authority to refrain from broadcasting a specified matter, so ministers could ban a topic. This is censorship in the sense used here: official restriction of broadcasts.
In practice the Act's duty of impartiality in news and current affairs sat alongside ministerial power, so how far RTÉ was independent was a constant source of conflict.

Seán Lemass saw television as a means of national development and public information, and he called RTÉ "an instrument of public policy". By this he meant that it should support the government's national goals, not that it should be a mouthpiece for the government.
The opposing view, held by many in RTÉ, was that a broadcaster serves the public only if it is free to criticise the government, because a station that cannot criticise cannot hold power to account.
The clash between these two views shaped the history of RTÉ in the 1960s and led to the crisis of 1971 and 1972.
notes.tip: On a documents question about Lemass, show what he wanted from RTÉ (support for government policy) and what the documents show about how he dealt with the Authority. Cite the document and its detail, and comment on its author and purpose when judging its value.

notes.b: Television filled the schedule with a mix of foreign programmes and Irish ones. The Irish programmes mattered most, because they showed Irish people to themselves.
points: Much early output was imported from Britain and the United States, including westerns, comedies and films, so imported programmes gave Irish viewers a view of life elsewhere.
Home-produced programmes covered news, sport, current affairs, drama, light entertainment and Irish-language material.
Gaelic games and other sport drew large audiences.
The Riordans, a drama about a farming family that began in 1965, was a hit with viewers, especially in rural Ireland, because it dealt with real issues of farming life and change.
Telefís Scoile, which began in 1964, broadcast programmes for secondary schools, bringing television into the classroom.
Irish-language programmes and news bulletins in Irish were part of the service from the start, though they took a small share of airtime and often had a small audience.
RTÉ also raised standards for Irish drama and music, and helped writers, actors and musicians to reach a national audience.
notes.tip: Programme names alone score weakly, so for each one (such as The Riordans or Telefís Scoile) give the date and its effect on viewers.

notes.h: The Late Late Show and Gay Byrne
notes.b: The Late Late Show became the best-known programme on Irish television and a forum for national debate. It began modestly, but its willingness to discuss sensitive subjects made it a symbol of change.
points: The programme was first broadcast on Friday 6 July 1962 as a live summer filler, a programme meant only to fill the schedule, and it became a fixture.
It was a live talk show with guests, music and audience participation, and Gay Byrne presented it from 1962 until 1999, bringing an open-minded, humorous but probing style.

The show discussed subjects that were rarely talked of in public, including sex, marriage, contraception, unmarried mothers and the church, which is why it came to be seen as a force for liberalisation (the relaxation of controls on what could be discussed or done in public life).

In 1966 a quiz item for married couples led to the episode known as the Bishop and the Nightie: when Gay Byrne asked a wife, Eileen Fox, what she had worn on her honeymoon night, she said she had worn no nightdress, and the remark caused uproar.
Bishop Thomas Ryan of Clonfert condemned the programme, and other clergy and some viewers complained, while many viewers defended Byrne and the show, so the public split.
The incident showed that television could provoke public argument about morality and the limits of church authority, and it brought the Late Late Show to national attention.
notes.tip: For the 1966 incident, give the date, what happened, Bishop Ryan's condemnation and the way the public divided. Do not mix up this show with the Late Late Toy Show, which is outside this case study.

notes.h: Current affairs and clashes with government
notes.b: Serious current affairs programmes put RTÉ on a collision course with ministers. The government had the means to pressure the broadcaster, and it used them.
points: Seven Days, a current affairs series launched in 1966, used young producers and reporters to investigate housing, poverty, emigration and other social issues. It began in autumn 1966, shortly before Lemass left office, but most of its run fell under Lynch.
Ministers resented programmes that criticised policy, and they complained to the RTÉ Authority, which was under pressure to restrain current affairs.
A Seven Days programme on illegal moneylending in 1969 led to a government-ordered inquiry and a row over RTÉ's independence, after which current affairs was reorganised.
From 1969 the Troubles made coverage of Northern Ireland a major source of conflict between RTÉ and the government, which feared that broadcasts would encourage violence.
The government held financial and legal power over the broadcaster, since it appointed the Authority and could change the law, so RTÉ could resist pressure only so far.
notes.tip: Do not confuse Seven Days (current affairs, 1966) with This Week (radio, 1972, the Mac Stíofáin interview). Use Seven Days as evidence that RTÉ challenged authority and that the state could respond.

notes.h: Effects on rural life, religion and politics
notes.b: Once most homes had a set, television began to change everyday life and public attitudes. The effects were felt in the countryside, in the Church's influence and in how politicians won votes.
points: Television altered how evenings were spent, since people stayed at home to watch rather than go to dances or visit neighbours, and it reduced the isolation of rural communities.
It brought national and international news and sport into every home, so people in the countryside had access to the same culture and entertainment as city people.

Programmes on social issues exposed viewers to arguments about contraception, divorce and the church that censorship had kept out of print. This contributed to secularisation, the decline of religion's influence on public life and personal behaviour.

Church leaders such as McQuaid were concerned about the effects of television on faith and morals, but the church also used television to broadcast Mass, the Angelus (a traditional prayer) and religious programmes.
Politicians had to learn to use the medium: party leaders appeared on television to speak directly to voters, and campaigns began to focus on television appearances and image.
Viewers' reactions varied: many welcomed the new window on the world, while others, including some clergy and traditionalists, saw it as a threat to Irish values.
notes.tip: When asked about the impact of television, link each effect to a specific example and a consequence. Strong answers separate short-term entertainment from longer-term change in attitudes.

notes.h: The crisis of 1971 to 1972: Section 31 and the Authority
notes.b: Coverage of the Northern conflict led to the first serious use of the government's powers over broadcasting. Two separate events, a year apart, showed how limited RTÉ's independence was.
points: 1. On 1 October 1971 the Minister for Posts and Telegraphs, Gerry Collins, issued the first order under Section 31, directing RTÉ not to broadcast material that could promote the aims of organisations advocating violence.
RTÉ journalists protested that the order restricted reporting of the Troubles and argued that the public had a right to hear different views.
2. On 19 November 1972 the radio programme This Week broadcast an interview by Kevin O'Kelly with Seán Mac Stíofáin, chief of staff of the Provisional IRA, who was arrested the same day.
3. The government regarded the broadcast as a breach of the Section 31 order, and in late November 1972 Collins dismissed the whole RTÉ Authority and appointed a new one.
4. O'Kelly was later prosecuted and jailed for refusing to identify Mac Stíofáin's voice in court.
The sacking caused protests by journalists and in the Oireachtas (the Irish parliament), and it raised the question of whether a state broadcaster could report freely.
The order was renewed and widened in 1976 under Conor Cruise O'Brien, then Minister for Posts and Telegraphs, and it was not renewed in 1994.
notes.tip: Keep the order of events clear: the first Section 31 order (1971), the interview (1972) and the dismissal of the Authority (late 1972) are different events. Be ready to explain why they showed limits on RTÉ's independence.

notes.b: Byrne was the presenter of The Late Late Show and the best-known broadcaster in Ireland for decades. He is both a participant in the change of the 1960s and a figure that historians use to judge it.
points: Gay Byrne was born in Dublin in 1934, worked in Britain in the 1950s and then returned to Irish radio and television, becoming a presenter on Telefís Éireann in its first years.
He presented The Late Late Show from 1962 to 1999 and a radio programme from the early 1970s, which gave him a wide audience in every part of the country.

He was a participant in the change of the 1960s: his questions to guests and audience on sex, marriage and religion set the agenda for debate, and he hosted the 1966 episode and handled the controversy.
He generally avoided taking sides, presenting himself as a neutral host, yet his willingness to air subjects that the church or the government preferred to avoid had a liberalising effect.
Contemporaries were divided: many welcomed him as a modern voice, while others, including some clergy and traditionalists, attacked his programme as a danger to morals.

Historians regard him as a major influence on how Irish people talked about sexuality, the church and social issues, while noting that he was also shaped by changes already under way, so television reflected change as well as causing it. He died in 2019.
notes.tip: Do not confuse Gay Byrne the broadcaster with Gabriel Byrne the actor. In a personality answer, give what he did with dates, then how others judged him, then how far he led or reflected change.

notes.h: Differing contemporary and later views of RTÉ's role
notes.b: People disagreed about what RTÉ was for. Each group judged it by its own interests, and historians now weigh these views against one another.
points: The government and Lemass: RTÉ should help to modernise the country, explain official policy and support national aims, and ministers expected a degree of cooperation from its Authority.
RTÉ journalists and producers: a national broadcaster should be free to investigate and criticise, and many saw ministerial pressure as censorship.

The Catholic Church: television was a powerful influence on the young that needed to be watched, and bishops and priests objected to some programmes, though the church also valued the airtime given to religion.

Language activists: Irish-language output was too small a share of the schedule, and imported English-language programmes, mostly from Britain and the United States, risked weakening the language further.
Rural viewers: programmes such as The Riordans showed their own lives, while others thought the city-based producers misrepresented the countryside.
Politicians outside government: opposition parties complained of bias in favour of the government, and some felt that the Authority was too ready to give way to ministers.
Robert Savage, in A Loss of Innocence? Television and Irish Society, 1960-72 (2010), argues that television reflected changes already under way and also accelerated them.

John Horgan, in Broadcasting and Public Life: RTÉ News and Current Affairs, 1926-1997 (2004), shows that the relationship between the state and the broadcaster was complicated rather than simply one of control.
notes.tip: Strong answers acknowledge that television reflected changes already under way as well as speeding them. Cite a named historian where you can.

notes.h: Assessment: did RTÉ entertain, challenge and change its viewers?
notes.b: The best way to judge RTÉ is to take the three verbs in turn and set the achievements against the limits. Examiners reward a clear judgement backed by named programmes and events with dates.
points: Entertained: it brought sport, drama, light entertainment and music to a national audience, and many programmes, such as The Riordans (1965) and The Late Late Show (1962), were hugely popular.

Challenged: current affairs and chat shows questioned authority and exposed issues that were taboo, such as contraception, poverty and the Northern conflict, as in Seven Days and the 1966 Late Late Show episode.

Changed: viewers had a wider view of the world, attitudes to church and state became more questioning, and the habit of national debate grew, which marks a move towards liberalisation and secularisation.

Limits: the government held strong powers, and Section 31 (1971) and the dismissal of the Authority (1972) showed that independence was fragile, while Irish-language programmes struggled for audiences.
Contemporary view: viewers welcomed the entertainment and new voices, while the church and government saw risks in the programmes.

Later view: historians argue that television both entertained and challenged, and that it sped up changes in attitudes to religion, sexuality and authority, while acknowledging that television was one cause among several.
Other causes of change mattered too: education, emigration, EEC entry and the economy all helped to alter attitudes, so television should not be given all the credit.
notes.tip: Open with a clear judgement, then give paired points on all three verbs, each backed by a named programme or event with a date. For essays that pair RTÉ with another force, state which mattered more and why.
